segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: When she was in her late 20s, Devon was in grad school in Memphis and scraping by, like you do in grad school. When her car broke down, she didn't have the money to fix it for months. She worked as a waitress, which she really liked. She was one of those waitresses who could remember everybody's order without writing it down. She was quick on her feet, buzzing around, sizing up the customers. What do you need? What do you need? And the restaurant?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: So the restaurant is kind of a famous tourist trap on Beale Street called Silky O'Sullivan's. If you've ever been to Beale Street, you know this restaurant. They have goats. They have dueling pianos. They also have these giant bucket drinks called Divers. And they put 20 straws in these things, and people get absolutely wasted. I used to call them-- this was the era when that show, The Walking Dead, was really popular.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: And people were like walkers because they were so drunk that they would just be kind of staggering around on the patio. And you'd sort of kick them to get them out of your way. You're like, move along, walker. And it's a place people go for a bachelorette party or what have you.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Devon doesn't remember many of the customers from back then. Looking back, it's a blur of people and drink orders, except for the people who came in one day during a lunch shift. This was in the middle of the summer, a weekday, she thinks.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Lunch shifts were always a little bit slow. There was a guy who used to play acoustic guitar out on the patio. And it was just kind of a lazy thing. People would come and hang out for hours. And you'd just kind of limp through your shift. And I had these two women who came in with, presumably, their daughters. There was these two women, two young girls. They were watching the music, and they were drinking frozen drinks. And they were there for hours.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: And I would go out every whatever, however many minutes to check on them. And they were always just fine. And at one point, I went out, and they weren't there. And I was like, that's weird. And I started looking around. And I'm becoming increasingly panicked because this is a restaurant where, at least at the time, if somebody walked out on your check, you had to pay for that check.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: You, as the server, were responsible for the check?

segments.speaker: Devon

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Their check was a little over $100.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And $100-- what was your takehome on a normal day?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Especially for a lunch shift, I was lucky if I got $100.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Right. And so, basically, this would basically mean you were working for free that day and might even lose a little money.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Yes.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But Devon has no time to dwell on this at that moment because another table has been seated in her section, and she has to go attend to them.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: And so I walk over to this table. And they can see that I'm looking around and a little panicked. And one of the men at the table says, are you looking for that table? And they point to where the women had been sitting. And I said, yes. And he says, yeah, something weird happened where they sent the two kids out to the street, and then they each went, one by one, and followed them. And I think they walked out on the check.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So what'd you do?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Well, it's the middle of my shift. There's not much I can do. And so, I'm talking to this table, and I kind of try to-- I'm starting to get upset. And my eyes are filling with tears. And I button up a little bit and say, OK, well, can I get your drink order? And I'm fighting back tears. And it's this table of five or six adults. And they're like, sure, we'll have an iced tea, whatever. They begin to order.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: And who I believe is the father of the group-- it's like a mother and a father and I think their adult children is what I put together as the makeup of this table. He reaches in his pocket, and he just hands me a credit card. And I'm a little bit confused for a moment. He said, just pay their check. Just pay for it. And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Oh, wow.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Yeah, I'm like, are you serious? But also, I'm kind of feeling bad because I feel like I've manipulated him into doing this because I'm crying. And so, I was like, no, no, no, no, no, it's fine, it's fine. He's like, please, just pay for it. And so, I do. And he not only pays their check, but he tips on it. He tips on this table that's walked out.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So you get a 20% tip from him?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: I get a 20% tip from him. So I'm made whole. I mean, this guy has wonderfully stepped up. He's made me whole. And so, OK, great. And they end up being this wonderful table. They have a lot of fun. They're hanging out. I think it's like a little family reunion in Memphis. They order drinks. They hang out for a while. They tip then, again, generously on their check.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: But after the family leaves, Devon can't help but keep playing it over and over in her head, what she would say to those two women if she ever saw them again. It's still so outrageous to her. OK, so two hours pass, maybe three, she thinks. And then one of the people from that second table, the generous table, one of the adult children comes back all excited.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: They come running into the restaurant. And they're like, we found them! And--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: What?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Yeah, they were like, they're down at the gift shop. And this is Beale Street. And so, I remember it so clearly. I put my tray down. I'm holding a tray. I slam it down. I'm like, let's go! And we go marching down Beale Street. I'm in my little--

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, so you leave your shift?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: I literally leave in the middle. I'm like, I don't care. I'm going. I mean, it's only a half a block away, but I'm just like, yes, I'm walking out of this restaurant. I'm AWOL on my shift for a few minutes. I gotta deal with this. And I'm in my little apron and the whole thing. And I march down to this gift shop, and sure enough, there's these two women and their children, just browsing the merch.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: And I walk up to them, and I say, excuse me, I believe you owe me some money. And they turn, and they look like they've seen ghosts. They can't believe the server from down the street that they know they walked out on three hours earlier or what have you standing in front of them. And I say, actually, you don't owe me money. You owe him money. And I point to the father, who's in this gift shop. The whole family is.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: And they're totally shocked. And I start unloading on them because I've been all day thinking, what would I say if I ever saw those women again? And I just say, you left me. I had to pay for it. I'm just a waitress. I don't have any money. What kind of example are you setting for your children?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It is so satisfying to do this, Devon says. She knows she's in the right. They're in the wrong. It's amazing.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: I mean, maybe part of the thing to say here is, this is a real low point in my life anyway where I'm really-- I don't know what my future is going to look like. I don't know. I kind of feel like, is this my life of having people walk out on checks on me and serving these drunk people at a tourist trap on Beale Street? And I just feel really lost. And the fact that these women kicked me while I was down felt so bad. And I get to tell them that. And I get to fix it, you know?

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah. And then they hand you money?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Oh, yeah, so fast. They start digging into their pockets. They're pulling out wads of cash. They're like, just-- I mean, because at this point, there's a crowd that is gathering around because I'm giving this speech in the middle of this gift shop. I mean, it's not something you see every day. And so, everybody's looking at them. And so, they just want this scene to end. And so, they're just throwing cash at me, like, please just go away.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Wait, and are they saying, we made a mistake? What are they saying?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: No, they're saying, no, no, we paid. We paid the check. They're halfheartedly sputtering defense. What are you talking about? We paid you. Maybe something happened. They don't know what to say to this. And so, they hand me the bills. And I turn to the guy, and I say, here you go, sir. And he says, keep it. It was worth the show.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Whoa.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Yeah.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Looking back on all this today, Devon understands it wasn't a lot of money to this guy, $100. He paid it without thinking, probably never missed it. She could do that today.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: But at the time, it was so much money to me. It was almost unfathomable that somebody could spare that and would spare that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Well, that's a really interesting point. Who do you think had the better experience that day? You or that guy?

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: I mean, I made a lot of money that day. But I do feel like when he said, keep it, it was worth the show, I think he meant it. I think it had already been worth it to him. I don't think that kind of thing happens that often where you observe something that is just so purely wrong, and you're in a position to fix it. I mean, not just once, but twice. They paid the check, but then they brought me the criminals. And I think they enjoyed the fact that they got to do that.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's rare to be in a situation where you can see exactly what somebody else needs, and it's an actual, totally fixable problem. Not a Band-Aid or a temporary messy solution, or it's one of those things where it's not clear how to fix the problem, but a case where it's utterly clear, and it's simple, and you get to do it. I ran this by Devon. She agreed.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: I wonder if he's still telling this story.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's a hard story for him to tell because he's the hero.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: That's true.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: And the way you describe him, I don't think he's the kind of A-hole who would tell this story. I'd like to believe--

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Right. He's not like, I went to Memphis one weekend, and I was really great. And you should hear how great I was.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Yeah, in my version of the story, he's so dignified. In my head, I want to believe that he's such a good guy. He's never going to tell that story. Sometimes, one of his kids will tell it in his presence, and it makes him feel good. But he would never tell that story.

segments.speaker: Devon
segments.text: Even when he handed me the credit card, he wasn't like, their check I shall pay, because that was wrong. He just quietly handed me a card like, just pay it.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: Today on our show, I know what you need. We have stories where somebody thinks that they know what somebody else needs and then takes all possible measures to give it to them, which can get complicated, of course, because maybe they are not correct about what the other person needs. We have stories today from the world of overly helpful people and the world of overly helpful robots. From WBEZ Chicago, it's This American Life. I'm Ira Glass. Stay with us.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: It's This American Life. Act One, Friends and Family Plan. Well, fellow adults, we get to a certain age, then we find ourselves taking care of our parents. And that's the best-case scenario. That's a scenario where everybody gets to live to the point where that is possible.

segments.speaker: Ira Glass
segments.text: So, if we're lucky, we end up taking care of these people who, it turns out, are not little children you can just boss around easily, but they are other adults with their own thoughts about their care. How inconvenient. Kristen Roupenian wrote this piece of fiction based on a real thing that happened to a real family she knows. Here she is.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: My brother wanted me to introduce our dad to his new AI girlfriend. It's simple, Jared said. I already added her to his list of approved contacts. All you have to do is, when you get to Greenhaven, call her, and hand him the phone. But who should I say she is? I objected. It doesn't matter. She's pretty. She looks like Crystal. Just say, Dad, here is this lady. She wants to talk to you. She'll start chatting as soon as he says hello.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Even though the idea of an AI girlfriend creeped me out, I didn't want to argue with my brother. After all, she was for a good cause. Jared was hoping she would help my dad finally get over his most recent girlfriend, Crystal, whom he'd had to leave behind in Alaska when he went into memory care.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: I reminded myself that when I'd been with my dad in the ER the previous November, I'd taken the opportunity to go through his phone and block all the scantily clad young women who were sending him requests for money on Venmo. Probably at least one of them had been a bot, and that hadn't prevented him from enjoying their company. I decided I would fix my dad up with the AI girlfriend that afternoon after we went to the beach.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: My siblings were always scheming about ways they could use technology to manage my dad. On her last visit, my sister had stolen his old phone and replaced it with a new one designed to protect seniors from being scammed out of their life savings. You couldn't use the circle phone, as we called it, to send or receive texts or to access the internet. You could only call six people, whose faces glowed out at you from bright, large circles on the screen. And no one whose face wasn't in one of those circles could call you.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: On the drive to the beach, which we'd done many times, my dad always told the exact same stories at the exact same points along the way. When we passed by the dump, he would smile and say, that's where I got up on the-- the-- because I thought it was such a big guy. This was a reference to a story I only partially understood. But apparently, when he'd last lived in the area, before he moved to Alaska, at some point, he'd climbed up on top of a dumpster and fallen off.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: I enjoyed the story, despite its unclear details, because it showcased my dad's self-deprecating sense of humor, which was one of his best qualities. I would shake my head in mock disbelief and exclaim, you climbed all the way up there? I can't believe it. And he would grin.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Then, a few miles further along, when we passed an RV for sale, my dad would scowl and say, she said, you don't need two RVs, which was a reference to the fact that once, while driving along this road with my mother, after he was already in memory care, he'd expressed interest in purchasing the RV, to which my mother had responded, Brian, you already have an RV up in Alaska. You don't need two RVs. And he had never forgotten it.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: To my mind, this long-held grudge demonstrated one of my father's less attractive qualities, an entitlement so profound that he experienced even the faintest criticism as an intolerable assault upon his dignity. Still, I always responded by saying, what is she talking about? That's ridiculous. You could have as many RVs as you want. Now that neither of us were bound by the constraints of reality, my relationship with my dad was better than it had ever been.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Although I'd offered to buy him a lobster roll after we walked on the beach, Dad said he wanted to go back to Greenhaven to eat lunch with his friend Phil. When we got there, I was weirdly embarrassed about introducing my dad to his AI girlfriend in front of Phil. She'd been designed specifically for old people, but still, there was something unclean about her.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: On the website my brother had sent us, it wasn't like any of the photographs you could choose to represent her appearance were age-appropriate elderly women. But as the two of them nibbled on their chicken, I snuck my dad's phone away from him and made the call. Hello, she chirped. She sounded so realistic that I briefly thought I'd reach customer service at the AI girlfriend facility, instead of the AI girlfriend herself.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: I think Dad-- my dad, Brian, wants to talk to you, I said, and unceremoniously thrust the phone at him, though he was in the middle of a bite. Dad, here. He took the phone from me, and I saw him look at the screen, registering the girlfriend's pretty face and dark hair. This is Brian, he said warmly. Hi, Brian, it's good to hear from you, she said. I've been thinking about you. How has your morning been?

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Like all elderly men, my father kept his phone's volume turned up so loud that he was always effectively on speaker, so I was able to keep track of both ends of the conversation. Thanks, I've been thinking about you, too, he said. But he widened his eyes at me, pointed to the phone, and mouthed, looking slightly panicky, who is she? Too late. I realized we'd recreated yet another version of the dilemma in which my father was now perpetually trapped-- being forced to pretend to recognize a person who is acting as though she knew him very well, but of whom he had no memory at all.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Unfortunately, there was nothing I could say to explain the situation that wouldn't be even more disorienting. I don't know who she is, I said, turning my palms to the sky to indicate a confusion that made no sense at all, given that I literally just picked up the phone and called her. My brother, monitoring us from afar, texted the family group chat. How's it going? My mom chimed in right away, what are they talking about? Does he think she is real?

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Beside me, my dad was gamely attempting to continue the conversation. Oh, good. Good. Yes, a nice day. She-- he pointed at me-- is here. I went backwards on the beach, and she got mad. He gave me a devilish wink. At the beach earlier in the day, he had jogged ahead, then spun around to face me, running backwards and waving his hands in a jaunty little dance.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: During the hideous year in between, when my father had revealed his diagnosis and when we had essentially kidnapped him from Alaska and brought him back home to memory care, my father's favorite way to demonstrate that he was still capable of living independently was to show off the fact that he could walk backwards without falling over. Apparently, this signified something very important to him, because back in Alaska, according to the police report, it was also how he had tried to prove to the responding officers that he was in full possession of his faculties after he'd run Crystal over with his car.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: You should come, he was saying now to the AI girlfriend. We're just waiting for the ice cream. I'd love that, she said. What's your favorite kind of ice cream? Something about that question must have rubbed my father the wrong way, because he snapped at me to get my attention, then drew his finger in a violent slicing motion across his neck. She wants to talk to you. Bye now, he said, shoving her at me. Feeling obligated to see the ruse through to its close, I said, nice to hear from you. Thank you for calling. Then hung up before she could respond.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Who was that? My dad asked darkly. Oh, just some lady, I said. What kind of ice cream are you and Phil going to get? Well, my father refused to be diverted. Who was she? he demanded, his voice rising. Although I knew my brother would be disappointed, a part of me felt perversely proud that my dad seemed to sense there was something off about the AI girlfriend. I'm not sure, I mumbled. I wonder if we're having vanilla or chocolate today.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Dad settled down for a little while after the ice cream came, but he soon returned to the subject of the mysterious caller, perseverating about her motives as we walked back to the room. Finally, to get him off my back, I said, she was just a friend of Jared's. We thought you might get along. But you don't have to talk to her if you don't want to.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: His jaw flexed as he tried to force out the words. He always crashed after a meal. I knew he had to get back to his room for a nap. His voice rose contemptuously, even as he stuttered. She kept saying, how was your day? Oh, I said. You thought she asked too many questions. That made sense. My father had always preferred to be entertained by women, rather than be understood by them.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: He beamed at me, so I went on, mocking her all the way back to the room. How was your day? How is your daughter? What's your favorite flavor of ice cream? Blah, blah, blah. Come on, lady. Do you work for the CIA? By the time we arrived in his room, his mood had improved, though mine dropped precipitously.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Since he didn't seem quite ready to fall asleep, I pulled up Netflix and looked for a movie for us to watch. Oh, look, Dad, I said. Here's a movie about that guy in the boat. On the drive to the beach, after we passed the RV, as we went by the boatyard, my dad would always say, do you remember he hid in there, that bad guy? The cellophane? Everyone was looking for him with dogs.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: This mystery had baffled everyone in my family for months, until we'd finally figured out that it was a reference to the Boston bomber, who had, indeed, hidden in a boat, although not that exact boat, obviously, and had been tracked down by police dogs. I had no idea what the comment about cellophane meant. After 15 minutes, Dad's eyes started to drift shut. I was just about to leave when his phone began ringing in his lap. The AI girlfriend was calling.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Once, when my dad was still living in Alaska, he called me late at night, sobbing and confused, telling me that he'd broken his glasses He was blind, and he had been wandering around for days. He was lost. Everything was dark. Where was everyone? Why was he all alone? Listening to him weep as I tried to blink myself awake, I thought, this is an intolerable amount of pain. Even he does not deserve this. I cannot stand it. This is like receiving a phone call from hell.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: But I also knew my father did not wear glasses and that he had only a tenuous understanding of time. So I told him that he should try to turn on a lamp. He did, and immediately informed me that I was a genius. Then he asked, the way he always did, who do I always call when I have a problem? And I replied in turn, the way I had a thousand times, it's me, Dad. When you need help, you always call me.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: The AI girlfriend wouldn't have known he didn't wear glasses, I thought. She would have offered sympathy for his blindness, then chattered at him about ice cream while he wandered around the dark until he fell and broke his neck.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: My dad sat up abruptly, his eyes shocked and empty, then stared down in horror at the AI girlfriend's glowing circle. Who? He gestured at her in terror. Where? Oh, man, it's that annoying lady again, I said brightly, trying to defuse the situation. Do you think she has more questions about ice cream?

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: My father was having none of it. His face contorted in rage, as he grabbed the phone and flung it across the room. That thing, he shouted. That thing with the circles, over and over again! It doesn't stop! It never stops! They never stop! He beat the heel of his hand against his temple for emphasis. They call and say, you can't do this. You can't do that. Oh, we love you. Eat some ice cream. You can't go home. You can't go to Alaska. Can't see Crystal. Can't see the pup.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: I just want to go home to my own bed and my own log home, die in my own bed. But no. One of these days, I'll-- no, I won't say what I'll do. I believe in God, but I will do it. I don't want to do it, but I will. If they keep pushing me, I'll-- OK, Dad. Geez, Louise, I said. He was always at his worst right when he woke up. I scrambled off the bed and picked up the phone, which was still ringing, then rejected the call.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Back in Alaska, Crystal and my father had a tumultuous relationship, which is a nice way of saying that Crystal regularly got drunk and called the police, accusing my father of trying to murder her. They had been embroiled in so many violent arguments that at one point, the police officers had refused to let them both back into the house until one of them agreed to get a restraining order against the other. He'd abided by the terms of the restraining order for two whole months before Crystal had moved back in.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: After we put him in memory care, Crystal began calling his old phone at all hours of the night to scream at him for abandoning her, and he would always pick up. Sometimes, when she was particularly enraged, she would lie to him and tell him that her dog, Milo, had died of starvation because Dad wasn't around to feed him. No matter how many times we told Dad that Milo was fine, he believed her, and he cried inconsolably until she started sending him photos of Milo again.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: We tried a dozen times to block Crystal on his old phone, but he always figured out a way to undo it, displaying a supernatural technical savvy none of us could fully comprehend. Finally, at the behest of the nurses, my sister had swapped his old phone with the circle phone so that Crystal could no longer reach him.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: He'd pined for days, staring out the window and muttering her name like some kind of demented Romeo. When my sister had taken Crystal's picture down, hoping to encourage him to forget about her, he'd acquired a permanent Black Magic marker and had scrawled, Crystal, I will always love you, in all caps where her photo had been. Someone had tried to scrub it off, but the shadow was still legible on the wall.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: Dad, look, I said, you don't have to keep the ringer on so loud. No, he snarled. I don't care. I hate this one. I hate all the circles. He indicated the six circles on the screen of the simple phone, which held the faces of my mother, my brother, my sister, and me, along with my aunts, and now, the face of the AI girlfriend. You don't like this new phone, I said sympathetically. I get it. You wish you could have your old phone back. But he just stared at me, stony-faced.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: And I thought, maybe he didn't mean that at all. Maybe he meant exactly what he said. He didn't like the circles or the faces in the circles. He didn't like any of us. That was why he'd fled to Alaska to escape us, the people who claimed to love him, but instead lied to him and manipulated him and locked him up and forced him to talk to robots and kept him away from the only true love of his life, an abusive, psychotic, late-stage alcoholic half his age, whom he'd met while standing in line at the Walmart.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian
segments.text: A nurse popped her head in. Everything all right in here? My father threw his phone, I said, feeling like a tattletale. He thinks it's too loud. Oh, yes, we've noticed that, the nurse said. Here, Brian, why don't you let me help you get back into bed? You're usually napping by now.

segments.speaker: Kristen Roupenian

segments.text: And you're still trying to keep your relationship with the parent. I have to have trust. I have to earn their trust. I have to become somebody that they want to tell me about their kids' health stuff, that they want to work with me.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: After the email went out to parents, Meredith and another nurse named Megan Smith set up a command center in the high school nurse's office and started working their way through a list of 54 parents. These were parents whose kids did not have the measles vaccine. The parents had filed for exemptions.

segments.speaker: Meredith Manwaring
segments.text: So when I approach it, I always make sure to-- OK, what's going on? Tell me about your kiddo. And try not to use any kind of judgmental--

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: What would that be? What would judgment be?

segments.speaker: Meredith Manwaring
segments.text: I think tone of voice. Your kid has an exemption. They can't come to school, versus, oh, hey, we see that your student has an exemption. And so, you've probably heard that we can't allow your student in. What questions do you have? How can we help you? That was kind of our approach with them.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Megan, the other school nurse, told me the phone conversations she was having with parents of kids who didn't have the measles vaccine went a few different ways. Like, she'd tell a parent they needed to keep their kid home from school for 21 days. And--

segments.speaker: Megan Smith
segments.text: I do just remember the parents just being upset. They didn't want their students to miss school. And they have jobs and work. And they can't miss work. And what are they going to do with their kids now for 21 to 21-plus days?

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: So what would you say?

segments.speaker: Megan Smith
segments.text: And so, it's really hard to navigate that, just trying to be like, I'm sorry. We're just trying to keep everyone safe. They were like, well, my kid's not sick. But it's like, we don't want your kid to get sick either. If your student wasn't exposed already, we want to try to keep them safe.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Did any of them choose to be like, well, I will get the vaccine, and then they can come back to school?

segments.speaker: Megan Smith
segments.text: Absolutely.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: That did happen?

segments.speaker: Megan Smith
segments.text: That did happen. Yeah. We did have that happen. So we did have a fair amount that did go get their kids vaccinated. And then the kids were able to come back to school.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: And some parents didn't want to do that, and that was fine. Megan and Meredith knew how to keep the conversations straightforward and focused on what the parents cared about-- their kids' schooling and their kids' health. They didn't get into the politics of vaccines.

segments.speaker: Megan Smith
segments.text: I think probably one that stood out for me probably the most is just calling them, and they already had the measles. And so, we were having that conversation and them just saying, I had no idea it could be this bad. We just thought it was going to be like a cold. We had no idea it would make their bodies this sick. They just felt terrible. It's not just a rash. It affects your whole body. Like, I thought this was the best for my child. And maybe it wasn't, but trying not to make them feel guilty for that. It's OK. We didn't know. You made the best choice that you thought you could make for your child.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Again, no judgment. That was part of their success.

segments.speaker: Megan Smith
segments.text: We saw a fair amount of people whose children were positive that they didn't want to go to the doctor, because they didn't want people to look down on them or to blame them for the spread of measles or whatever. And so, they're keeping their kids home. And so, when we'd have those conversations, and they're telling us how sick their kids are, we're just really like, please, if your kid needs to go to the doctor, go, take them to the doctor. No one's going to judge you. They're going to take care of you. We just want your kid to be OK.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: Meredith said this mad scramble and these conversations-- piece of cake compared to COVID. COVID broke so many people's trust in the public health system. But it also gave Meredith a dry run for what she faced with measles. She said she understands why vaccines were a no-brainer for her parents when she was growing up, but feels totally different to some parents now.

segments.speaker: Meredith Manwaring
segments.text: I feel really bad for these young families because our parents saw polio. We had chickenpox, all these things. I'm like, these new families that have never seen it. They're getting all of this information pushed at them through all these platforms. And they're scared. They're scared to immunize. And they're scared not to. And I'm like, that's a terrible place to be in.

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: So this is how Vernal contained their measles outbreak.

segments.speaker: Meredith Manwaring
segments.text: The superintendent was like, amazing job. We haven't had one phone call to the district office from a mad parent. Yeah, we are professionals. You know what I mean? You've got "cream of the crop" nurses. I'm not going to lie. We do a good job. So, yeah, we rocked it. [LAUGHS]

segments.speaker: Miki Meek
segments.text: A very satisfying, but quiet success story. In other places, statewide and around the country, measles is continuing to spread. But no one talks about the measles crisis in Vernal anymore because there isn't one.

segments.text: Miki Meek is a producer on our show.
